title: From 'Riverdale' to Eternia: How Camila Mendes Trained to Wield Teela's Sword
summary: When Camila Mendes first held Teela's sword on the set of 'Masters of the Universe,' it wasn't just a prop—it was the culmination of months of grueling training. 'I had a lot of sword training,' Mendes told Space.com. 'I had to do some rifle training because of her rifle staff.' For the actress best known as Veronica Lodge on 'Riverdale,' stepping into the role of Eternia's Royal Guard captain meant transforming herself physically and mentally. 'Through all the weight training and stunt training that I had to do, I felt like I was literally becoming Teela,' she said. The process mirrored the character's own backstory: Teela trained from a young girl to become the fierce warrior she is. Mendes's preparation went beyond learning fight choreography. She delved into Teela's emotional core, describing her as a 'parentified child'—someone forced to grow up too fast and shoulder immense responsibility. 'She's had to take on so much responsibility and hasn't really had a break,' Mendes explained. 'I feel like that's something a lot of people this day and age can relate to.' That inner conflict plays out in Teela's strained relationship with her father, Duncan (Idris Elba), the former captain who went down a darker path, and in her awkward reconnection with childhood friend Adam, aka He-Man. The film itself is a wild blend of sci-fi, fantasy, and 80's nostalgia, complete with flying Griffins and epic sword fights. But at its heart, it's a story about a young woman balancing duty with vulnerability. Mendes, no stranger to sci-fi after 'Riverdale's' time-travel and alternate-dimension plots, found that the weapons were key to unlocking the character. 'These weapons are an extension of her in a way, so that really helped me sort of finalize her,' she said. 'Masters of the Universe' opens worldwide on June 5, promising a spectacle where Teela proves she's just as mighty as He-Man.
why_it_matters: This story shows how an actor transforms through intense dedication, and the character Teela’s struggle to balance responsibility and personal feelings reflects pressures many teens face when forced to grow up fast or manage adult problems at home.

background_read: Camila Mendes became famous playing Veronica Lodge on the teen drama 'Riverdale' (a show that mixed high school life with wild sci-fi twists), but her new role as Teela connects to a much older franchise.

Teela first appeared in the 1980s animated series 'He-Man and the Masters of the Universe' as the captain of the Royal Guard of Eternia; she was a fierce warrior and often saved the day alongside He-Man.

The 1987 live-action film 'Masters of the Universe' starred Dolph Lundgren as He-Man and Meg Foster as a different version of Teela, but it was not a box-office hit; this 2026 reboot brings a fresh, modern take with characters like Duncan, played by Idris Elba (a British actor known for his roles in 'Thor' and 'Star Trek: Discovery').
Sword training for a fantasy movie like this involves learning stage combat—safe but realistic-looking fight choreography—often taught by stunt professionals.

perspectives.description: Fans of the original 1980s cartoons and new viewers alike can see a powerful female warrior on screen, and Mendes's realistic, emotionally layered Teela offers positive representation. Her rigorous training inspires young people to take physical challenges seriously.

Some may argue the film is yet another nostalgia-driven reboot cashing in on a beloved brand without truly fresh ideas. The pressure on Mendes to do her own stunts also raises safety concerns in an industry that often puts actors through extreme regimens.

The film blends 1980s fantasy nostalgia with modern themes about mental load and parentification, reflecting a cultural shift in our understanding of childhood responsibility. The character's emotional arc mirrors a trend in blockbuster cinema where even larger-than-life heroes are given relatable inner struggles.

If 'Masters of the Universe' succeeds, it could launch more female-led fantasy franchises and encourage Hollywood to invest in characters that balance strength with emotional depth. Mendes’s training journey might also set a new standard for actors preparing for physically demanding roles.
